title: Christmas, all twelve days
tomorrow: why would anyone write on their front door in chalk?

cards: The day after Christmas: trees already on the curb, playlists switched back, the stores rolling out red hearts for February. As far as the stores are concerned, Christmas is over. For the Church, it has barely started.
The old count runs twelve days, from Christmas to the eve of Epiphany. And the Church's own calendar goes further still, keeping Christmas Time all the way to the feast of the Baptism of the Lord.

teach.b: Luke has a line for this. After the shepherds leave, after all the noise, "Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." The feast doesn't end when the visitors go home.
It settles in and gets turned over, slowly. That's the logic of the twelve days.

teach.h: THE OCTAVE: EIGHT DAYS AS ONE.
teach.b: Christmas Day doesn't end at midnight: the Church keeps it as an octave, eight days celebrated as one long feast, closing with the solemnity of Mary, Mother of God.

The days in between are crowded: Stephen, stoned for his faith in Acts; John the apostle; the Holy Innocents; the Holy Family. Then the twelfth day opens onto Epiphany. Homes fill the stretch with taste and smell.
In Abuela Rosa's kind of kitchen, that's tamales on Christmas Eve and a ring-shaped sweet bread saved for the magi's feast.

teach.h: A TABLE THAT SMELLS LIKE COMPANY.
teach.b: Elsewhere, it's oranges and cloves, a pot of soup that never seems to empty, a house that smells like company.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in the Church's calendar, the day after Christmas is still Christmas, and so is the next, and the next.
Keep feasting isn't permission to overeat.
It's a refusal to let joy be a one-day event. Mary didn't stop pondering when the shepherds left, and the season gives the joy room to sink in.

how: Catholics keep Christmas as a season: the octave of eight days, the feasts that follow, Epiphany, and Christmas Time until the Baptism of the Lord, often with family meals and visits through the days after Christmas.

the four quiet weeks of waiting

games.q: your little cousin cries the day after Christmas because 'it's over.' what's the Church's answer?
o: it isn't over: the feast keeps going for days, so let's keep celebrating.
it is over, but there's always next year to look forward to.
Christmas was really only ever about the presents anyway.
games.why: the Church keeps Christmas as an octave and a season. the day after Christmas is still Christmas.

practice: Find something with a smell or a taste you can reach: an orange, a spice jar, a piece of bread, a cup of coffee. Hold it close and take it in slowly, turning it over the way Mary pondered.
Let it bring back one Christmas table you've sat at, and the faces around it. If you pray, you can give thanks for one of them by name.

wordCard.voice: Christmas. Not a day but a season: the feast that keeps going, through the octave and past the twelfth day.

orig.note: Greek, from Luke 2:19: pondering in her heart.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: keep feasting. The shepherds went home, and the feast kept going without them.
